deep.reconstruction:
The page is one sheet of a large hand-ruled table of quadratic residue characters between primes. Each row is labelled by a prime modulus p. The upper block runs through every prime from 439 to 521. The lower block uses the selected primes 523, 557, 571, 577, 599, 613, 617, 641, 653, 659, 677 and 701. Each column is labelled by a prime q from 2 to 89. A small circle at (p,q) means q is a quadratic residue mod p, i.e. the Legendre symbol (q/p)=+1. No other text or computation appears.

The neighbouring sheets fit this reading. The previous sheet (folio 14) has rows 191–433 against columns 829–997. The next sheet continues rows 439–541 against columns 97–223. Together they form a large two-way table of (q/p) for primes up to about 1000.

Verification (mine), using the supplements (2/p)=+1 iff p ≡ ±1 mod 8, (3/p)=+1 iff p ≡ ±1 mod 12, (5/p)=+1 iff p ≡ ±1 mod 5, and quadratic reciprocity otherwise:
- Column 2 is marked exactly for 439, 449, 457, 463, 479, 487, 503, 521, 577, 599, 617, 641. These are exactly the listed primes ≡ ±1 mod 8.
- Columns 3 and 5 are likewise marked exactly as the supplementary laws require, in every row, including the lower block.
- Rows 439, 457 and 521 match my full Legendre-symbol computation exactly.
- Row 439: residues among q ≤ 89 are 2, 5, 7, 11, 13, 19, 29, 53, 61, 71, 73, 83.
- Row 457: 2, 3, 7, 17, 19, 29, 47, 67, 73, 79.
- Row 521: 2, 5, 11, 13, 29, 31, 37, 47, 53, 59, 71, 83.
- Rows 443 and 499 also agree with the computation once the image is read correctly; the machine transcription mis-read them (see corrections).

The lower block (523–701) was only begun. Columns 2, 3, 5 are filled correctly and completely for the listed rows. Columns 7 and 13 have only isolated entries: 7 at 701 and 13 at 677, both correct. Many residues are not yet entered there, e.g. 7 is a residue mod 523, 557 and 613; 13 is a residue mod 523.

The pen strokes join circles in horizontally adjacent columns (consecutive column primes) or vertically adjacent rows (consecutive row primes). They appear to be a visual aid for spotting runs and patterns, with no further mathematical content.

Red crayon '15' and the circled '8' / crossed-out '40.18' are archival foliation, not Gauss's mathematics.

Purpose: an empirical table of the quadratic character, of the kind behind Gauss's inductive discovery and checking of quadratic reciprocity (1795–96) and akin to Table II of the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801). Table II lists, for prime moduli below 1000, which primes up to 97 are residues.
errors: No errors found in the entries I checked: rows 439, 443, 449 (columns 2/3/5), 457, 499, 521, and columns 2, 3, 5 for all rows; apparent discrepancies are transcription errors.

The lower block (rows 523–701) is incomplete rather than wrong. Only columns 2, 3, 5 are systematically filled; columns 7 and 13 have isolated correct entries; residues such as (7/523)=(7/557)=(7/613)=(13/523)=+1 are not marked.
The lower block skips many primes (541, 547, 563, 569, 587, 593, 601, 607, 619, 631, 643, 647, 661, 673, 683, 691); the selection criterion is not evident.

results.what: Table of the quadratic character (q/p) for prime moduli p = 439..521 (complete) and selected p up to 701 (partial), against primes q = 2..89; part of a larger two-way table of primes below 1000.
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table (cf. Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, Table II)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, Table II); earlier residue tables by Euler and Legendre

results.what: Empirical data consistent with the supplementary laws for 2 (p ≡ ±1 mod 8), 3 (p ≡ ±1 mod 12) and 5 (p ≡ ±1 mod 5), and with quadratic reciprocity.
results.modern_name: Supplementary laws and law of quadratic reciprocity (empirical verification)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured), Legendre (1785/1798), first complete proof Gauss 1796

deep.surprise_reason: A correct working table of quadratic residues of exactly the kind Gauss is known to have computed for the Disquisitiones and his discovery of reciprocity. It is routine computational material, with no new result.
